tickets.title: High-Balance Accounts
tickets.description: Writes a query to retrieve active checking accounts with balances above $5,000.
tasks: Writes a query to retrieve active checking accounts with balances above $5,000.
learning_objectives: Understand relational database design and PostgreSQL features.
tickets.evaluation: `compare_result_set(actual, expected)` `check_projected_fields(actual, included=['customer_id', 'account_type', 'balance', 'status'], excluded=[])` `check_sort_order(actual, 'balance', 'DESC')` **[A] Correctness (40 pts)**: 40 pts if exact result set matches; 20 pts if balance filtered correctly but status active check is missing. **[B] Optimality (30 pts)**: 30 pts if query executes in `< 5ms`. **[C] Quality (20 pts)**: 20 pts if keywords are uppercase (`SELECT`, `FROM`, `WHERE`); 10 pts if lowercase.
common_mistakes: Forgetting semicolons at the end of statements.
Using reserved keywords as column names without quotes.
hints: Remember to use GROUP BY for aggregate functions like SUM, COUNT, or AVG.

solution.query.sql:
SELECT customer_id, account_type, balance, status
    FROM accounts
    WHERE account_type = 'checking'
      AND status = 'active'
      AND balance > 5000.00
    ORDER BY balance DESC;

tickets.title: Suspended VIP Audits
tickets.description: Locates suspended high-risk customers who still have checking accounts in the database.
tasks: Locates suspended high-risk customers who still have checking accounts in the database.
learning_objectives: Understand relational database design and PostgreSQL features.
tickets.evaluation: `compare_result_set(actual, expected)` `check_command_used("JOIN")` **[A] Correctness (40 pts)**: 40 pts for finding correct matching records. **[B] Optimality (30 pts)**: 30 pts if query targets indexes. **[C] Quality (20 pts)**: 20 pts for structured join conditions.
common_mistakes: Forgetting semicolons at the end of statements.
Using reserved keywords as column names without quotes.
hints: Remember to use GROUP BY for aggregate functions like SUM, COUNT, or AVG.

solution.query.sql:
SELECT a.id AS account_id, c.name, c.email, a.balance
    FROM accounts a
    JOIN customers c ON a.customer_id = c.id
    WHERE a.status = 'suspended' AND c.risk_level = 'High'
    ORDER BY a.balance DESC;

tickets.title: Daily Transaction Volumes
tickets.description: Computes total transaction volume (using absolute amount values) and average transaction size per completed type per day.
tasks: Computes total transaction volume (using absolute amount values) and average transaction size per completed type per day.
learning_objectives: Understand relational database design and PostgreSQL features.
tickets.evaluation: `compare_result_set(actual, expected)` `check_command_used("ABS")` `check_command_used("GROUP BY")` **[A] Correctness (40 pts)**: 40 pts if daily sums match; 20 pts if aggregates exclude failed status check. **[B] Optimality (30 pts)**: 30 pts if grouping matches indexing. **[C] Quality (20 pts)**: 20 pts for clear column aliases (`tx_date`, `total_volume`).
common_mistakes: Forgetting semicolons at the end of statements.
Using reserved keywords as column names without quotes.
hints: Review the PostgreSQL documentation for exact syntax.
Test your queries in smaller chunks first.

solution.query.sql:
SELECT
      type,
      DATE(created_at) AS tx_date,
      COUNT(*) AS tx_count,
      SUM(ABS(amount)) AS total_volume,
      ROUND(AVG(ABS(amount)), 2) AS avg_size
    FROM transactions
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY type, DATE(created_at)
    ORDER BY type, tx_date;
